title: Communicative Language Teaching: Getting Students Talking
summary: Learn what communicative language teaching (CLT) is, how to increase Student Talking Time (STT), which activity types get students speaking, how to manage group work and how to correct errors well.

sections.h: Welcome to Week 5: how you teach
p: In Week 4 you planned your lessons. This week you look at the way you teach them. Good plans fail if students do not get a chance to use English. The aim of this week is simple: more student talk, better tasks and better resources.
This week you will learn:
• Communicative Language Teaching (CLT) and how to use it.
• Task-Based Learning (TBL) and how to run a task cycle.
• How to teach speaking for Paper 3.
• How to make your own reading, speaking and writing tasks.
• How to adapt endorsed textbooks safely.
• How to build checklists so students can check their own progress.

b: Bring one real text from a newspaper or website.
Think of one class where students are quiet. Why?

p: CLT is a way of teaching where students learn English by using it to communicate. The main goal is that students can use the language in real situations. It is not only learning rules.
Key ideas of CLT:
• Meaning comes first. Students use the language to do something real: ask, explain, agree, decide.
• Fluency and accuracy both matter. Fluency means communicating without long stops. Accuracy means using correct grammar and words.
• Students work together in pairs and groups. They are not only listeners.
• The teacher is a guide, not only a speaker. The teacher plans the task, listens and helps.
• Language is learned in context, with real or realistic topics.
• Errors are normal. They show that learning is happening.
Myths about CLT:
• 'CLT means no grammar.' Not true. Grammar is taught, but through use.
• 'CLT is only speaking.' Not true. Reading and writing tasks can be communicative too.
• 'CLT is noisy and out of control.' It can be well organised, with clear tasks and time limits.

b: Students fill in gaps with the correct verb: not very communicative.
Students interview each other and note answers: communicative.
Students read a text and then decide with a partner which advice is best: communicative.
Students copy sentences from the board: not communicative.

sections.h: Student Talking Time and Teacher Talking Time
p: Student Talking Time (STT) is the time students spend speaking English. Teacher Talking Time (TTT) is the time the teacher speaks. Many trainers suggest that in a speaking lesson students should speak for at least half of the time, and much more in some activities. The Cambridge Speaking test is only 10 to 15 minutes, but the practice takes many hours.
Why STT matters:
• Students learn to speak by speaking.
• They try new words and see what works.
• They get ready for Paper 3, where they must talk for two minutes alone.
How to measure STT:
• Ask a colleague to watch a lesson and tick every time a student speaks and when the teacher speaks.
• Record 10 minutes on a phone and listen. Count how many students speak.
• Count how many different students speak, not only how long.
Teacher talk is not bad. Clear instructions, good models and feedback are needed. But the teacher should speak only when it helps learning.

b: Who spoke most in the last 10 minutes: me or my students?
How many students did not speak at all?
What could I change to give them more time?

sections.h: Ten ways to increase Student Talking Time
p: Try these ideas.
• 1. Pair work first. In a class of 40 students, pair work gives 20 speakers at once.
• 2. Think, pair, share. Students think alone for 30 seconds, tell a partner, then share with the class.
• 3. Give wait time. Wait three to five seconds after a question.
• 4. Short instructions. Say them once, show an example and check with one question.
• 5. Ask open questions. 'Why do you think that?' is better than 'Is it true?'.
• 6. Do not repeat or rephrase every answer. Let students listen to each other.
• 7. Use roles in groups: speaker, note-taker, timekeeper, reporter.
• 8. Use mingle activities. Students walk around and speak to many partners.
• 9. Use a 'three before me' rule. Students ask three classmates before asking the teacher.
• 10. Put students in rows or circles that help them face each other.

b: Use pairs and rows, not whole class questions.
Teach students signals for starting and stopping.
Use the same pair activities every week so students know the routine.

sections.h: CLT activity types for IGCSE ESL
p: Here are common CLT activities with examples that match the exam.

• Information gap: each student has different information and must ask questions. Example: Student A has the morning timetable of a school trip, Student B has the afternoon. They ask and complete the full timetable.
• Opinion gap: students give their own opinion and may disagree. Example: 'Should students wear a uniform?' Tell your partner your view and one reason.
• Reasoning gap: students decide between options and explain. Example: Choose the best gift for a friend from five options. This links to Paper 3 Part 2.
• Role play: students act a situation. Example: ask for a refund for a product with a problem.
• Jigsaw: each student reads a different part of a text and tells the others.
• Survey or mingle: students ask the same question to many people and record the answers.
• Problem solving: groups plan a school event with a budget.
• Discussion with roles: one student chairs, one summarises, others give views.

b: Student A: You know the cost of a theatre trip and the time. Ask B about the museum trip.
Student B: You know the cost of a museum trip and the time. Ask A about the theatre trip.
Then decide together: which trip is better value, and why?

p: Group work can go wrong if it is not planned. These steps help.
• Give a clear task and outcome. Say what students must produce.
• Set a time and show a timer.
• Make groups of two to four. Larger groups mean fewer speakers.
• Give roles when needed.
• Mix levels for helping, or group by level for challenge. Change groups often.
• Move around the room. Listen. Do not sit.
• For early finishers, have an extension: 'Now tell your partner two reasons to disagree.'

• For students who share a first language: ask them to use English for the task, and agree rules. If they must use the first language to understand, allow it for ten seconds and then return to English.
• For shy students: give them time to prepare notes, work in pairs first, and praise effort.

b: Task, outcome and time are clear.
Roles are given.
I have a plan for early finishers.
I will listen and collect errors.

p: Monitoring means walking around and listening while students work. You have three jobs: help, listen and collect.
• Help: answer a question or give a word. Keep it short.
• Listen: notice good language and errors. Write down five examples on paper.
• Collect: do not interrupt the task for every error.
Correct in the right moment. When the task is about fluency (such as a discussion), delay correction. Wait until the end.
Delayed correction method:
• Write 5 to 6 sentences from students on the board without names. Include both good sentences and sentences with errors.
• Ask the class to find and fix the errors in pairs.
• Praise a student who said something good.

In accuracy practice, correct more quickly. Use techniques such as: repeating the sentence with a questioning tone, using fingers to show word order, giving a hint ('past tense?'), or asking a peer to help.
Do not correct everything. Choose errors that block understanding or that appear again and again. This matches the exam, where marking credits what students can do.

b: Student said: 'I really wanted to take place in the event.'
Better: 'take part in the event.'
Student said: 'Yesterday I go to the shop.'
Better: 'Yesterday I went to the shop.'

p: Some teachers worry that CLT will not prepare students for the exam. In fact the exam rewards communication. The Speaking test is a real conversation, and writing marks go to clear, developed content. The examiner report for June 2024 says strong responses are well developed, use a range of structures and vocabulary, and have clear organisation.
A balanced week might be:
• Two lessons of communicative tasks, with a focus on talk and writing.
• One lesson of exam skills with past paper exercises.
• One lesson of language focus and feedback.
This way students get both fluency and exam technique.

b: Communicative tasks: about half of the time.
Exam skills: about a quarter.
Language focus and feedback: about a quarter.

activity: Record 10 minutes of one of your lessons on your phone, or ask a colleague to observe. Count the teacher talk and student talk. Then plan one information gap activity for your next lesson and try it. Write three sentences on what happened.

check.q: Which is an example of an opinion gap?
o: Students say whether they agree that school should start later and give a reason
Students fill in a gap with a verb

check.q: When should you correct errors in a fluency discussion?
o: After the task, using delayed correction
Only at the end of the term

check.q: What is the best way to increase Student Talking Time in a large class?
o: Use pair work and short instructions

title: Task-Based Learning: The Willis Framework and a Full Lesson
summary: Understand task-based learning (TBL), follow the Willis framework of pre-task, task cycle and language focus, study a complete speaking lesson and a writing lesson, and compare TBL with PPP.

p: In task-based learning (TBL), students learn English by doing tasks. A task is a piece of work where students use English to reach a real outcome. They focus mainly on meaning. They use their own words.
A real task has:
• A clear goal or outcome, such as a list, a decision, a plan or a short talk.
• A reason to communicate.
• A gap: something students need to find out, decide or create.
• Meaning first, with language support second.
Examples of tasks:
• Choose the best place for a class trip and tell the class why.
• Make a list of ten rules for a school club.
• Solve a problem: you have missed the last bus. What can you do?
• Plan a school event with a budget and present it.

b: Fill the gaps with the correct preposition: exercise.
Decide with a partner which of two options is better and explain why: task.
Write the past tense of ten verbs: exercise.
Prepare a one-minute talk on a hobby and give it to a partner: task.

p: Jane Willis described a well-known TBL framework in her 1996 book A Framework for Task-Based Learning. It has three stages: pre-task, task cycle and language focus.
• Pre-task: The teacher introduces the topic and the task. Students recall words they know. The teacher may play a recording of others doing the task. Time: 5 to 10 minutes.

• Task cycle: This has three parts. First, the task: students do it in pairs or groups while the teacher monitors and does not correct. Second, planning: students prepare to report to the class what they did or decided. They ask the teacher for help with language. Third, report: students present or exchange their written work, and the class compares results.

• Language focus: Students look at the language of the task. First analysis: find and discuss useful words and structures in a text or recording. Then practice: the teacher leads exercises on useful words and patterns. Time: 10 to 15 minutes.

img.alt: A flow diagram of the task-based learning framework: pre-task, task cycle with task, planning and report, then language focus
img.cap: The Willis task-based learning framework: pre-task, task cycle (task, planning, report) and language focus.

b: Students use language first, then study it.
The teacher focuses on form after the task, based on what students needed.
The report stage gives a real audience.

sections.h: A full TBL speaking lesson: the school trip decision
p: This lesson practises Paper 3 Part 2 skills: comparing two options and saying which one you prefer. It lasts about 60 minutes.

Pre-task (10 minutes). The teacher shows pictures of a museum and a national park. Students brainstorm words: exhibition, guide, tickets, hiking, wildlife, view. The teacher plays or reads a short model talk of a student comparing two options, and students note phrases such as 'On the one hand' and 'I would rather'.

Task (10 minutes). In groups of three, students decide which trip the class should take. Each says one advantage and one disadvantage of each option. The group must reach a decision and prepare two reasons.
Planning (8 minutes). Each group prepares to report. They write key words, not a script. The teacher helps with language but does not correct mistakes in the discussion.
Report (10 minutes). Each group tells the class its decision in 30 to 60 seconds. The class votes on the best reasons.

Language focus (15 minutes). The teacher writes sentences from the task on the board, good and with errors. Students find and fix the mistakes. They underline phrases for comparing and preferring. Then they practise in pairs with new options (a concert or a football match).
Follow-up: each student records a two-minute talk at home on a new card.

ex.t: Why this lesson works for Paper 3
b: Students meet comparison language before they need it.
They do the task twice: in the group and again in the report.
The teacher uses real errors from the lesson.
The follow-up copies the real exam talk.

sections.h: A TBL writing lesson: a short report
p: TBL works for writing too. Here is a 60 minute lesson for a report on a school event.

Pre-task (10 minutes). Show headings of a report: Introduction, What was good, What could be better, Conclusion. Students read a short model and underline useful phrases. Brainstorm: what words can we use for 'good' and 'bad'?
Task (15 minutes). In groups of three, students list what was good and what could be improved at a real school event (sports day, assembly, exam week). They choose three ideas and write notes.
Planning (10 minutes). Each group plans a short report in four paragraphs. They decide who writes which paragraph and help each other with language.
Report (10 minutes). Groups exchange drafts. Readers underline two good phrases and one thing to improve.

Language focus (15 minutes). The teacher shows frequent errors and phrases that make the report formal ('It would be helpful if...', 'I would suggest that...'). Students correct and rewrite. For homework, each writes a 120 to 160 word report on their own, based on the group notes.

b: Students share ideas in a group.
They write alone for the exam style.
They get feedback twice: from peers and from the teacher.

p: PPP stands for Presentation, Practice, Production. The teacher presents a language item (such as the past simple), students practise it in controlled exercises, then produce it in a freer task. TBL changes the order: students try the task first, then focus on language.
PPP strengths:
• Clear, simple to plan.
• Good for beginners and for specific grammar.
• Students feel safe because they know what to say.
TBL strengths:
• More real communication and talk.
• Students use their own words and show what they already can do.
• Language teaching follows student needs.
TBL challenges:
• Needs more careful task design.
• Can be harder to manage in large classes.
• Students who like clear rules may feel unsure at first.

A good plan for the exam class: use both. Use PPP for a clear structure that students often get wrong (for example conditionals or the passive). Use TBL to build confidence and fluency, as in Paper 3.

b: Students never use the past tense in speaking: short PPP then a TBL task.
Students are shy and use short answers: TBL with pair tasks.
Students need a model of an email: present a model and practise, then produce.

p: Use this checklist to build your own tasks.
• Does the task have a clear outcome (list, plan, decision, talk)?
• Do students have a reason to talk (a gap or a choice)?
• Is the level right? A little challenging but possible.
• Is there a time limit?
• Is there a topic that students know or care about?
• Can the teacher see the result?
• Is there a chance to report to others?
Types of tasks:
• Listing: brainstorm and make a list.
• Ordering and sorting: put items in order or in categories.
• Comparing: find similarities and differences.
• Problem solving: find a solution.
• Sharing personal experience: tell stories.
• Creative tasks: write a poster, a quiz or a short play.

b: Students finish too early: add a second stage or a harder question.
Students use their first language: give a reward for English and give a role to each student.
Weak students stay silent: pair with a patient partner and give sentence starters.
The teacher worries about grammar: plan the language focus for the end.

p: Link every task to an exam skill. For Paper 3: Part 1 tasks are personal interviews, Part 2 tasks are comparison talks and Part 3 tasks are opinion discussions. For Paper 1: writing tasks are emails and reports.
A termly plan could be:
• Weeks 1 to 4: TBL tasks based on Part 1 type questions (personal topics).
• Weeks 5 to 8: TBL tasks based on Part 2 cards (two options).
• Weeks 9 to 12: TBL tasks based on Part 3 questions (opinions and discussion).
Keep timing in mind. Students must prepare for one minute and talk for up to two minutes in Part 2, so practise this exactly in the report stage sometimes.

b: Does my task have an outcome?
Does it prepare for an exam task?
Will I give feedback after?

activity: Write a full TBL lesson plan for a task of your choice, using the Willis framework. Include the pre-task, task, planning, report and language focus with timings. Try it with a class, and note two good sentences and two errors you will use in your language focus.

check.q: What are the three stages of the Willis framework?
o: Pre-task, task cycle and language focus

check.q: Where does the teacher focus on language form in TBL?
o: After the task, in the language focus
Choose the best of two trips and tell the class why

title: Teaching Speaking for Paper 3
summary: Use the June 2024 teacher's notes and the examiner report to teach speaking for Paper 3: the test format, what strong and weak talk sounds like, a language bank, practice routines and a mock speaking day.

p: Paper 3 is worth 40 marks and takes about 10 to 15 minutes per student. It is done in English, recorded in full and marked by the teacher. Students speak to the teacher or examiner alone.
The parts and times (from the June 2024 teacher's notes):
• Introduction: about 1 minute. Not assessed.
• Warm-up: 1 to 2 minutes. Not assessed.
• Part 1, Interview: 2 to 3 minutes. Assessed. Three questions on one topic.
• Part 2, Short talk: 3 to 4 minutes, including 1 minute to prepare. The student talks alone for up to two minutes about the card. Assessed.
• Part 3, Discussion: 3 to 4 minutes. Assessed. Questions linked to the Part 2 topic.
The marks are 10 each for Grammar, Vocabulary, Development and Pronunciation, applied across all three parts.

b: No notes in the room and no dictionaries.
They may ask for clarification at any time.
The examiner chooses the card, not the student.
They get a card only for Part 2.

sections.h: What the teacher's notes tell us
p: The 2024 teacher's notes contain ten Speaking Assessments, A to J. Each has a warm-up, a Part 1 topic with three questions, a Part 2 card with two options, and Part 3 questions.

Topics in the series (Part 1 topic and Part 2 card): cooking and inventions; staying healthy and a school newspaper; being helpful and a holiday abroad; your local area and a sports event; jobs and listening to music; art and giving a presentation; clothes and being environmentally friendly; animals and ways of learning; popular music and lifestyle; free-time activities and studying a story.
Look at the pattern of the three Part 1 questions:
• Question 1 asks about now or habits: 'Can you tell me something about the food you usually eat at home?'
• Question 2 asks for a past story: 'Can you tell me about a time when ... and what happened?'
• Question 3 asks for an opinion: 'Do you think ... ? Why? Why not?'

The Part 2 card always gives two options and asks students to compare and say which they prefer and why. The tasks use different focus: how useful, how easy or difficult, how enjoyable, the advantages and disadvantages.
Part 3 questions are opinion questions on a wider theme, such as 'Do you agree...?' or 'What are the advantages and disadvantages of...?'
Keep these notes confidential for the live series. Use your own cards that follow the same pattern for class practice.

b: Give students a past topic and ask them to predict the three Part 1 questions.
Check against the pattern: now, past, opinion.

sections.h: What strong and weak talk sounds like
p: The June 2024 examiner report for Speaking gives clear pictures. Here is a summary in simple words.
Strong Part 1 answers:
• Use the right tense for each question: present for habits, past tenses for a past event, future or 'should' for opinions.
• Use a range of simple and complex structures, such as modals, conditionals and comparatives.
• Give examples and details.
Weak Part 1 answers:
• Stay in the present tense for a past story.
• Give one or two short sentences and repeat words from the question.
Strong Part 2 talks:
• Start with a short introduction and say how the talk will be organised.
• Talk about both options, with advantages and disadvantages.
• Use linking words to move between ideas and finish with a clear preference and a reason.
Weak Part 2 talks:
• Talk about only one option.
• List only advantages for both.
• Do not say which option they prefer.
Strong Part 3 answers:
• Develop ideas with precise vocabulary and examples.
• Refer back to earlier points.
Weak Part 3 answers:
• Give relevant but very short answers with simple words.
The report also says many students did not give a past story when asked, so listen carefully to the tense of each question.

b: Listen to the tense in the question and answer in the same time.
Talk about both options.
Say which you prefer, and why.
Keep talking for the whole two minutes.

p: Give students phrases they can use. They need to practise until they are natural.
Starting the talk (signposting):
• 'I'm going to talk about two options: ... and ...'
• 'Both options have advantages and disadvantages, so let me start with...'
Comparing:
• 'On the one hand... on the other hand...'
• 'Compared with..., ... is more...'
• 'The main difference is that...'
Giving reasons and examples:
• 'because', 'since', 'so', 'which means that', 'for example', 'for instance'.
Giving an opinion:
• 'In my opinion', 'I believe', 'I'd say that', 'To be honest'.
Speculating and conditionals:
• 'If I went to..., I would...', 'It might be...', 'I suppose that...'
Past stories:
• 'It was last year when...', 'I was walking when...', 'I had never seen...', 'I used to...'
Buying time:
• 'Let me think...', 'That's an interesting question.', 'What I mean is...'
Finishing:
• 'So, overall I would choose... because...', 'In the end, I prefer...'

b: Give each student a card with a phrase and a task.
Students use the phrase in a one-minute talk.
The partner tallies each time it is used.

p: Plan short activities for each criterion.
Grammar (10 marks)
• Practise the tense that goes with each question type.
• Do short drills: change present to past, make conditional sentences, add a relative clause.
• Encourage complex structures (conditionals, relative clauses, passive) but do not make students afraid of mistakes.
Vocabulary (10 marks)
• Teach topic sets (health, travel, work, environment, technology).
• Teach collocations and phrasal verbs.
• Aim for precise words, not only fancy words. 'Infuriating' is better than 'annoying' only if it fits.
Development (10 marks)
• Teach the pattern: point, reason, example.
• Use extension prompts: 'Can you tell me more?', 'Why?', 'Can you give an example?'
• Practise talking for two minutes without stopping.
Pronunciation (10 marks)
• Work on clear sounds, word stress and sentence stress.
• Teach intonation: rising and falling to show meaning and feeling.
• Record students and let them listen to themselves.
Remember that pronunciation is its own criterion. A student with simple grammar can still have clear pronunciation and earn marks for it.

b: Tongue twisters for sounds.
Minimal pairs for confusing sounds.
Read a sentence five ways to show five feelings.
Underline stressed words in a paragraph and read it aloud.

p: Short, regular practice beats one long mock.
• Starter (5 minutes, every lesson): a Part 1 question. Pairs ask and answer. Rotate question types: now, past, opinion.
• Midweek (15 minutes): one Part 2 card. One minute to prepare, then partners talk for two minutes each while a third student times and listens.
• End of week (15 minutes): Part 3 questions in groups of four with a chair and a note-taker.
• Monthly: a recorded talk to listen to and mark with the four criteria.
Use a visible timer. Students must feel two minutes. Many students speak for only 45 seconds the first time.
Use your own cards. Write new ones each month. Use topics from the students' real life.

b: 30 seconds: say it once.
One minute: say it with a reason.
Two minutes: say it with a reason, an example and a comparison.

p: A mock before the real test builds confidence. Plan it like the real thing.
• Choose a quiet room and test the recording device.
• Prepare cards for Part 2 and question lists for Part 1 and Part 3.
• Start the recording with your name, the student's number and name, and the date, as in the real test.
• Use the scripts from the teacher's notes.
• Time each part. Do not let a student run beyond the time.
• Follow the prompts in the notes if a student does not start or stops early.
• Mark with the four criteria. Use best fit and decide the level and then the mark within the level.
• Listen again to a sample with a colleague and compare.
Marking problems found in the June 2024 examiner report:
• Some centres were generous when students spoke naturally but used a narrow range of structures.
• Some marked severely because of accent when the pronunciation was clear.
• Many did not mark pronunciation on its own evidence.
• Some marked for quantity of speech even when the answer was not relevant.

b: Give each student two strengths and one target.
Plan a lesson for the common weaknesses.
Keep the recordings to compare progress.

sections.h: Supporting students who find speaking hard
p: Some students are shy. Some have a small vocabulary. Others get nervous. Help them in steps.
• Start with pair work, then groups, then the teacher.
• Give sentence starters for the first minute.
• Let them rehearse with a partner before speaking in front of the class.
• Use recordings at home so they can listen and try again.
• Praise effort and clear sounds, not only perfect grammar.
• Show them that mistakes do not stop communication.
• Teach them to ask for clarification, which is allowed in the test: 'Could you repeat that, please?'
For stronger students: ask them to include a conditional, to give a surprising example, or to challenge a partner's idea politely.

b: Support: sentence starters and prepared notes in the practice stage.
Core: a card and a timer.
Stretch: two complex structures and an extra example.

activity: Write your own Part 2 card in the Cambridge style with two options and a task sentence. Test it with two students. Record one talk. Mark it with the four criteria and list two strengths and one target.

check.q: What does Part 2 of Paper 3 require the student to do?
o: Talk alone about two options on a card and say which they prefer and why
Answer three questions about a topic
Discuss a picture with a partner

check.q: What is the main problem with weak Part 2 talks according to the examiner report?
o: They focus on only one option or do not state a preference
They use too many linking words
